parentsEn: Son of Bilha Haya and Avraham Shmuel
cvEn:
Yehuda-Baruh Grinfeld, son of Bilha Haya and Avraham Shmuel, was born on 21 Iyar 5739 in Haifa. He was the third child of his parents, brother to Hanoch, Shoshana, Yitzhak, David and Bracha.

When he was a year and a half old, the family moved to the community of Mevo Horon on the outskirts of Jerusalem, and later to the Givat Mordechai neighborhood of the capital. Yehuda studied at the Tzion Ezri state religious elementary school, at the Makor Hayim middle school, and at the Yeshivat Yerushalayim Lezeirim high school (ISHLAZ). He was a member and youth leader in the Ezra youth movement, in the Gigi branch.

After finishing high school, Yehuda spent about two years at the Atarat Kohanim yeshiva in Jerusalem.

On the first of Nisan 5759, he enlisted for compulsory service in the IDF and volunteered for the Paratroopers. Being upright, gentle and considerate, he found it hard to adapt to the military "mindset." After about a year and a half he left to study at the Ayelet HaShachar Hesder yeshiva in Eilat, where he studied for about three years.

Yehuda married Gabriella, and the couple made their home in Maaleh Michmash, in the Jerusalem area. Yehuda joined the Lenetivot Yisrael yeshiva, which was first located at the Tomb of Shimon HaTzaddik and later moved to Neveh David. In the month of Heshvan 5766, he began studying biotechnology at the Hadassah College.

Yehuda was a full and principled man, gentle, considerate and loving. He loved his family, his friends, the Land of Israel and the Torah. He loved to learn and to add to his knowledge, and he used every free minute for study and for reading books.

Yehuda had large blue eyes, and his face was usually lit with a smile and laughter. He radiated vitality and energy, and despite his seriousness he went along with life with grace, which endeared him to those around him. He stood out for his quietness, a quietness of fullness and depth that carried meaning. He was a good friend and made many friends. He had simplicity and pleasantness, and although he knew a great deal in many fields, he was never haughty. Yehuda was a pleasant conversationalist and could engage anyone "at eye level": great and small, educated and simple, religious and secular.

Yehuda was a peacemaker and kept away from quarrels. It pained him to see disputes, and he was willing to give up many things to bring peace to the family and to others. The family stood at the center of his life. He loved everyone very much, and throughout the years he served in the army and studied at the yeshiva he made sure to stay in regular contact with his immediate and extended family, and he made a point of calling his parents and grandmothers every Friday. After he started a family of his own, he invested greatly in the home, in its physical and spiritual sides alike. He was a full partner in household chores, and he played with and taught his eldest daughter, Re'ut Shulamit, and his younger son, Ron Aviḥai. Yehuda's plans to build a large family, to study for a master's degree and to keep growing were cut short before they could be realized.

Everything he did, he did seriously and thoroughly, with his whole heart and great investment. Behind everything he learned or created was a fundamental thought about the best way to do it, even things that other people did merely "to fulfill an obligation."

Yehuda showed diligence and stubbornness, and invested a great deal in everything he chose to do, as expressed in his studies and in many other things. It was very important to him to excel, and even things that did not come easily he struggled with and persisted in until he succeeded.

Yehuda was a Torah scholar. He loved to study Torah very much and endeavored to live by its light. He studied for many years at the yeshiva, and his friends and teachers testified that he was a true scholar.

He was humble and did not take credit for himself. He did not consider himself above others, and in many areas he regarded others as wiser and more accomplished, even when he was at least as good as they were. He always volunteered and joined in every good deed.

Yehuda loved to travel, especially rappelling trips in the Judean Desert. He toured all parts of the country with his family and friends, and often initiated and urged outings.

On the 8th of Av 5766, during the Second Lebanon War, he was called up under "Tzav 8" for reserve duty.

Yehuda fell in the Second Lebanon War, in a battle on the northern border, on the 12th of Av 5766, at the age of twenty-seven. A Katyusha rocket fired from Lebanese territory toward the Kibbutz Kfar Giladi killed him and his fellow members of the unit. Also killed were: Major Eliyahu Elkrief, Lieutenant Shmuel (Shmuliko) Halfon, Lieutenant Yossi Karkash, Sergeant First Class Shlomo (Shlomi) Buchris, Sergeant First Class Daniel Ben David, Sergeant First Class Moti Butbul, Sergeant First Class Ziv Balali, Sergeant First Class Marian Berkovitz, Sergeant First Class Roi Yaish, Staff Sergeant Shai Shaul Michelevich, and Sergeant Grigory Aharonov.

Yehuda was buried in the military cemetery on Mount Herzl. He left behind a wife, a daughter and a son, parents, three brothers and two sisters. After his death he was promoted to the rank of Staff Sergeant.

From the words written by Gilad Ben Shalom, Yehuda's study partner at the Hadassah College in Jerusalem, published in the college newsletter "Kol HaMichlala": "To our dear Yehuda and his grieving family, we sat together on the same bench. You always arrived determined to learn and succeed. You always knew how to ask at the right moment (if at all). You always understood and took the trouble to explain to all of us the lecturers and the mathematics behind them. You sat quietly and used every free minute; I never saw you waste a moment. If there was a short half-hour break, you were always in the classroom studying or calling your beautiful wife Gabriella, who came to the college, and together you drove home to Michmash. You managed to support a family, study five long days a week in biotechnology, meet all your assignments and also study Torah. We will miss you, Yehuda, with your bashful innocence, your goodness and your caring. At first we did not know you. We saw you arrive and sit in class in your green fleece jacket, with a brace on your injured shoulder. We talked among ourselves about reserve duty when they called me, and you said that although you had been exempted, if your unit needed you, you would go with them and do everything you could to ease their burden within the limits possible. And so it was you, who had not enlisted as a frontline fighter, who was struck down behind the lines by a painful and unnecessary death. You, who were the best in the class, with profound knowledge and especially with good manners, goodness of heart and true modesty. Yehuda, I will remember you and your good qualities, and I will carry with me all the moments and the blue of your eyes until the day I die."

On the website of the Ayelet HaShachar yeshiva, an outline of Yehuda's character was published: "Yehuda was among those of whom 'silence is a fence for wisdom' is characteristic, one of the rare people with a full inner world, whose humility is his strength. In the yeshiva, he was one of the builders of love of Torah, constant and persistent, one of those with 'long thoughts' who works with patience and builds his solidity and the foundation of his broad Torah on that basis. His place in the study hall was never vacant during his time at the yeshiva; he was one of the eternal lights of the city of Eilat, one who took responsibility as a true 'guardian of the city.' Thus, with persistence and consistency, he earned his place right beneath the seat of honor..."

Yehuda's family has created a memorial website in his name, where his life story, eulogies and photographs can be viewed. Website address: https://did.li/GGcDN.
